newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian coffee growers see brighter times ahead.
newsitem.headline: Colombian coffee growers see brighter times ahead.

text.p: Colombian coffee growers, hard hit by the twin effect of heavy debts and a strengthening peso currency, believe they can now see the light at the end of the tunnel.

A survey compiled by the Regional Center of Coffee Industry and Business Studies (CRECE), based in Manizales, regional capital of central Caldas province, shows coffee growers are optimistic that production and prices will rise in the second half of this year.

"The price gains in the first quarter of 1997 (which continued through into the second quarter) have generated great expectation among all those in the coffee sector...it is, however, premature to say that there is a bonanza in the world coffee market."

Of 3,440 coffee farmers questioned 54 percent said they thought their situation was improving while 34 percent said it was about the same as last year. About 20 percent said they thought the situation of Colombia's coffee industry would get worse.
Of those polled 48 percent said they thought this year's main coffee crop, from the harvest due to begin in September, would be better than last year.

Colombia's National Coffee Growers' Federation forecasts a harvest of about 10 million 60-kg bags for the 1996-97 coffee year, which begins with the main harvest of 1996 and runs until just before the main harvest of this year. The 1995/96 coffee crop was 12.9 million bags.

In the first half of this calendar year Colombia produced 4.7 million bags of coffee compared to 5.3 million in the same period last year. Short supplies, particularly in the first quarter of this year meant many growers were unable to take advantage of high international prices which skyrocketed to above $3 per pound.
About 57 percent of those surveyed said their income in the first quarter had been mediocre while 29 percent said it had been very bad. Just 14 percent said the first quarter had been good.

The National Coffee Growers' Federation forecasts a 12 million bag crop in the 1997/98 coffee year, which coincides with the view of 38 percent of those surveyed, who said the flowering period in advance of this September's main harvest had been very good while 45 percent said it had been regular.
Growers in northeast Santander, central Risaralda and southwest Huila and Valle de Cauca provinces were most confident of a good crop at the end of this year.

Among coffee growers' most pressing concerns, before the international price boom, was the high value of the peso currency which effectively cut the value of coffee exports in peso terms and high levels of indebtedness.

Although the peso is not seen weakening significantly against the dollar this year and could even appreciate, 75 percent of producers said they had benefited from a debt relief plan introduced by the government and the federation earlier this year.

Despite fears of a supply shortage of about 1.5 million bags in the 1996/97 coffee year, CRECE predicted there would be a glut of coffee on world markets in the medium to long-term with Mexico aiming to boost exports and Brazil looking to up production.
It also said Vietnam and Indonesia, where production costs are low, could provide stiff competition for markets in Japan and China.
CRECE warned that Colombia still had to face up to the need for a "structural transformation" of the industry, particularly by cutting costs, if it was to remain competitive in the long term.

The survey questioned 3,440 coffee growers older than 19 years old, of which 80 percent were males. About half those questioned had plots of three hectares or less while 21 percent had plots of between 10 and 20 hectares. No margin of error was given.
